newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: ANZ sees softer NZ dollar in first half of 1997.
newsitem.headline: ANZ sees softer NZ dollar in first half of 1997.

text.p: The ANZ Bank said on Thursday that the prospects for some modest depreciation of the New Zealand had been growing, with narrower domestic-foreign interest rate differentials a major factor.

Based on ANZ's expectations for a gradual rise in world interest rates in 1997 and assuming no near-term deterioration for New Zealand's inflation outlook, Chief Economist Paul Stewart expects the New Zealand dollar in trade-weighted terms to depreciate by around five percent by mid-1997.
The differential between New Zealand three-month interest rates and those of other dollar bloc countries had declined to two percent from around four percent in September.
"That gap is now close to levels prevailing in 1994 and 1995 and any further narrowing is likely to significantly reduce capital inflows into New Zealand dollar interest rates," Stewart said.
Foreign investment flows attracted by New Zealand's markedly higher interest rates have been a major factor underpinning the Kiwi's strength in the last 12 months.

Stewart said ANZ expects New Zealand's current account deficit to worsen from the 4.6 percent of GDP in September 1996 to between five and six percent this year, which could also put downward pressure on the currency.
"This is very much a perception issue, but investors may begin to question the vulnerability of the exchange rate to weakness if large trade and financing imbalances persist," he said.
Stewart said fears that planned extra spending by the new centre-right coalition government would put upward pressure on the Kiwi may not immediately come to fruition.

He said any response to extra spending was unlikely until late this year at the earliest and in the meantime, fiscal slippage could cause foreign investors to view New Zealand's economic fundamentals more cautiously.
